vignette: Six months ago, on a rain-slicked sidewalk three blocks from her home, a man steps from a darkened alleyway. The crowbar presses against her ribs, heavy and unyielding. At seventy-one, Mai has spent decades navigating high-stakes corporate litigation, yet in this moment her training offers no armor. She remembers the smell of wet asphalt and copper, the frantic buzz of the streetlights, the sharp command in the man's voice. She does not fight. She hands over her purse, walks away with bruised ribs and a hollow chest, and returns to her house. Her husband, Thong, holds her while her body shakes. In the weeks that follow, the courtroom feels impossibly distant. Mai built her career on precision, precedent, and the steady command of a room. Now, precision fractures the moment she considers walking alone after dusk. She locks every door three times, then twice again. She reroutes her morning walk away from the parks. When the landline rings after midnight, her breath catches, her pulse hammers against her throat before her fingers even touch the receiver. She tells herself the nervous system simply needs time to recalibrate. The recalibration never arrives. Tonight, she sits across from me in her sunlit study, a leather-bound casebook resting face-down on her knee. Her posture remains rigid, the kind of disciplined alignment that comes from forty-two years of opposing counsel, but her hands tremble as she reaches for her teacup. The steam rises, and she stares into it as if watching something burn. Her voice stays steady, trained by years of cross-examination, yet her eyes dart to the window. Every passing car headlight makes her shoulders tense. She describes the nights when sleep fractures into fragments of the assault. Never the full story, just the glint of metal, the scrape of gravel under boots, the sudden drop in temperature. She wakes gasping, pressing her palms against the mattress to prove she is back in her bedroom. Thong has learned not to wake her immediately; he leaves a glass of water on the nightstand and gives her space to orient herself. She appreciates his patience, though a quiet guilt pools in her stomach. She used to be the one who fixed everything, the one who argued until the logic settled. Now, logic feels like a room she can no longer enter. Mai still attends board meetings at the firm, but she sits at the end of the table, facing the door. She has delegated her litigation docket to junior partners, claiming it is time for a quieter phase of her career. The truth is less polite. Last week, while reviewing a discovery document, a client's file falls open, and the redacted name on a protective order triggers a wave of nausea so intense she has to leave the room. She tells me this without self-pity, merely stating it as fact, the way she once stated precedents. Her mind, once a finely tuned instrument for parsing statutes and building arguments, now scans every environment for exits. She catalogs them instinctively: the stairwell, the service elevator, the alley behind the law library. It is a habit she cannot unlearn, or perhaps one she no longer trusts to unlearn. The grandfather clock in the hallway ticks past eight. Mai closes her casebook, her fingers lingering on the brass clasp. She speaks of the garden she tends, how the hydrangeas will finally bloom this summer if she can just make it outside after dark. Thong has offered to accompany her, but she has not accepted. Instead, she sits in the quiet of her study, breathing through the tightness in her chest, waiting for the hour to shift, for the light to change, for the world to feel, even for a moment, like something she can navigate.
